newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Bossi proclaims independence for "Padania".
newsitem.headline: Italy's Bossi proclaims independence for "Padania".

text.p: Seccesionist leader Umberto Bossi, capping a three-day "independence march" to the sea, proclaimed a self-styled "republic of Padania" in Italy's affluent north on Sunday.

But the weekend campaign, with its quasi-religious ceremony, failed to attract anywhere near the million followers he had hoped would follow his progress from the Alpine source of the Po river. In Milan, 150,000 rightists demonstrated for unity.

Bossi, viewed by his followers as a visionary but by many others as an eccentric, accused the rest of Italy, the poorer, more rural south, of treating the north as a colonial vassal. "We, the peoples of Padania, do solemnly proclaim: Padania is a federal, independent and sovereign republic," the firebrand leader of the Northern League told thousands of supporters in a declaration delivered in Venice.

"And for support of this declaration we mutually pledge to each other our lives, our fortunes and our sacred honour," it concluded, echoing Thomas Jefferson's July 4, 1776 declaration of American independence.
Italian President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro warned Bossi he could face criminal action over his proclamation.

In a speech at an international trade fair in Bari, southern Italy, Scalfaro said the state intended to guarantee freedom of expression but could not tolerate "incitement to illegal acts". There has been little clarity among Bossi supporters of where the borders of a Padanian state would run and opinion polls suggest little popular enthusiasm for the scheme.
At the end of his speech, delivered in Bossi's trademark gravely voice from a quayside platform, an Italian flag was lowered and the green and white flag of his Padania was raised.
"We will give this Italian flag to a representative of the government of Rome," a speaker told the crowd.
As Bossi arrived, green-shirted supporters broke into cheers, sang their would-be republic's new "national anthem" and chanted "Forza Padania" (Go Padania!).
"We have nothing to lose," one speaker told the crowd, introducing Bossi as a virtual messiah who would free them from "bondage" by the rest of Italy.

As music by 18th century Venetian composer Tommaso Albinoni wafted over the lagoon, Bossi read the words taken from the opening lines of the U.S. Declaration of Independence: "When in the course of human events ..."
He continued: "The Italian state has compromised the heritage of the north ...with systematic exploitation."
Bossi accused the central government of Mafia collusion and corruption.
"For these reasons we are convinced that Padania can no longer stay in Italy," he said, adding that a "free Padania" had a role in Europe and would be an "asset" to world peace.
"We the people of Padania, with courage...will be the masters of our own destiny," he said. "We recognise the inalienable sovereignty of every people."
"The hour has come to build this great country...with love and hard work" he said.

Bossi, who arrived in Venice on a catamaran from the city of Chioggia at the southern end of the Venice lagoon, made his proclamation after the crowd heard speeches of solidarity from members of other separatist movements around the world.
They included speakers from Italy's German-speaking Altro Adige (South Tyrol) region, a Flemish speaker from Belgium, a Catalan from Spain and a Sardinian separatist.
Earlier on Sunday at least 150,000 Italians marched for unity at far-right rally held in Milan, the north's biggest city, in response to Bossi and his push for "independence".
The size of the peaceful pro-unity demonstration dwarfed a series of sparsely-attended League rallies held since Friday along the River Po, the route of Bossi's symbol-laden trek.

Smaller pro-unity rallies also took place on the Po itself, including at San Benedetto Po, where Greens party supporters flew a string of balloons across the river, and at Piacenza, where one banner read: "Free the North, but from the League".
Bossi's League has built its appeal on deep discontent in the north with high taxes and stifling centralised bureaucracy coupled with disillusionment with mainstream political parties.

It won an unexpected 10.6 percent of votes at last April's general election but failed to wrest the balance of power in parliament, a defeat Bossi's critics say explains his switch to a secessionist from a federalist agenda.
